title: Design File System
summary: The flat hash map passes LeetCode 1166 in five minutes. The segment trie is what the interviewer is actually asking for — here is the pivot, the code, the concurrency follow-up, and every edge case worth stating out loud.

blocks.title: What you are actually being asked
blocks.text: LeetCode 1166 is a *warm-up*. The interview question hiding behind it is: **model a hierarchical namespace so that lookup, insertion and every follow-up (`ls`, delete, quotas, watches) stays cheap.** Solve the literal problem in five minutes, then spend the rest of the hour on the structure that survives the follow-ups.
The problem
Design a file system that lets you create paths and associate a value with each one.

items: `boolean createPath(String path, int value)` — creates `path` and associates `value` with it. Returns `false` if the path already exists, or if its **parent** does not exist. Otherwise creates it and returns `true`.
`int get(String path)` — returns the value at `path`, or `-1` if the path does not exist.

blocks.text: A path is one or more concatenated strings of the form `/` followed by one or more lowercase letters: `/leetcode` and `/leetcode/problems` are valid; `""` and `/` are not.

blocks.title: Read the contract twice
blocks.text: Three rules do all the work: **the path must not already exist**, **the parent must already exist**, and **the root `/` is never a createable path** — it is the implicit parent of every top-level entry. Most rejected solutions get the third one wrong.
Clarify before you code
The interviewer is grading the questions as much as the code. Ask these, in this order:

items.title: Is the input already normalised?
items.text: Do I have to handle a trailing slash, `//`, `.`, `..`, or an empty segment? On LeetCode the input is clean — in the interview version it never is. Agree on a `normalise()` boundary and move on.

items.title: Is `createPath` on an existing path an update or a failure?
items.text: The stated contract says failure. Real filesystems say `EEXIST` unless you pass `O_TRUNC`. State which one you are building.

items.title: Do I need to enumerate children?
items.text: This is the pivot question. If `ls` / `listChildren` is ever coming, a flat map is the wrong shape and you should say so now, not in the follow-up.

items.title: Single-threaded or concurrent?
items.text: Changes the data structure choice, not just a lock. Ask early so the design carries it.

items.title: How many paths, and how deep?
items.text: 10^4 paths fits anywhere. 10^9 paths pushes you toward interning segments and off-heap storage — mention it, don't build it.

blocks.text: Requirements

blocks.caption: Scope agreed with the interviewer before writing any code.
rows: `createPath(path, value)` — create only if absent and parent present
The parent check is the whole problem
Sentinel, not exception — the contract says so
These are what kill the flat-map answer
Shared prefixes must not be stored twice
Safe under concurrent readers and writers
Standard follow-up at Amazon and Uber

blocks.text: Approach 1 — the flat hash map
Store the *whole path string* as the key. The parent is just a substring: everything before the last `/`.

blocks.title: This is a correct, accepted solution
blocks.text: Do not pretend it is wrong — that reads as rehearsed. Say what it *is*: **O(m) per operation** for a path of length `m` (you hash the full string), dead simple, and the right call if the API never grows. Then say what it cannot do.
Where it falls over:

items: **`ls("/a")` is O(n)** — you must scan every key in the map to find the children of one directory.
**`delete("/a")` is O(n)** — same scan, to find the subtree.
**Memory duplicates prefixes** — `/usr/local/bin/node` stores all 20 characters, and so does every sibling. `n` paths of depth `d` store `O(n · d)` characters instead of `O(distinct segments)`.
**Rename is O(n)** — moving `/a` to `/b` rewrites every descendant key.

blocks.text: Approach 2 — a trie over path segments

Split on `/` and make each **segment** a node. The path *is* the walk from the root. This is exactly how a real filesystem stores directory entries, and it is the answer the interviewer is steering you toward.
The critical detail people get wrong: this is a trie keyed on **segments**, not on characters. `/leetcode` is one edge labelled `leetcode`, not eight edges labelled `l`, `e`, `e`, `t`…

blocks.title: Trie after four createPath calls
blocks.caption: `/leetcode` → 1, `/leetcode/problems` → 2, `/leetcode/contest` → 3, `/usr` → 9. Shared prefixes are stored once; `hasValue` distinguishes a created path from an implicit ancestor.

blocks.text: Class design

blocks.title: Two classes, one responsibility each
blocks.caption: `TrieNode` knows about *structure*. `FileSystem` knows about the *contract* — the exists/parent-exists rules live there and nowhere else.
blocks.code:
classDiagram
    class FileSystem {
        -TrieNode root
        +boolean createPath(String path, int value)
        +int get(String path)
        +List~String~ ls(String path)
        +boolean delete(String path)
        -TrieNode walk(String path)
        -String[] segments(String path)
    }

    class TrieNode {
        -Map~String, TrieNode~ children
        -int value
        -boolean hasValue
        +TrieNode child(String name)
        +TrieNode addChild(String name)
    }

    FileSystem "1" o-- "1" TrieNode : root
    TrieNode "1" o-- "*" TrieNode : children

blocks.title: Why `hasValue` and not "value != -1"
blocks.text: A node can exist purely as an ancestor. If you encode absence as `-1` you cannot tell `/a` *created with value -1* from `/a` *never created* — and the moment the interviewer allows negative values your `get` starts lying. An explicit `hasValue` flag (or a boxed `Integer`) is the honest model. Interviewers watch for this.
createPath, step by step

blocks.title: createPath control flow
blocks.code:
flowchart TD A[["createPath(path, value)"]] --> B{"valid path?
starts with / and len > 1"} B -- no --> F[["return false"]] B -- yes --> C["segments = split(path, '/')"] C --> D["node = root"] D --> E{"more parent segments
left to walk?"} E -- yes --> G{"child exists?"} G -- no --> F G -- yes --> H["node = child"] --> E E -- "no, at the last segment" --> I{"last segment
already a child
with a value?"} I -- yes --> F I -- no --> J["create or reuse child
set value, hasValue = true"] J --> K[["return true"]] style F fill:#3a1f22,stroke:#f4696b,color:#f2f2f7 style K fill:#153229,stroke:#34d399,color:#f2f2f7

blocks.text: Walk every segment **except the last** and require each to exist — that is the parent check. Then handle the last segment: it must not already carry a value.
Try it
Run calls against a live trie. Watch how `createPath` refuses an orphan, and how a node created as an ancestor is still *not* a created path until it gets a value.

blocks.name: file-system-trie
blocks.title: Interactive trie
blocks.caption: Every call runs the exact algorithm above — the tree and the return value come from the same code path.

blocks.text: Complexity

blocks.caption: `m` = path length in characters, `k` = number of segments, `n` = number of stored paths, `c` = children of one directory.

blocks.title: Do not oversell the trie
blocks.text: Both are O(m) for `get`. The trie wins on **structure**, not on point lookup — and it costs you one `HashMap` object per node, which is real overhead when paths are shallow and never enumerated. Saying this out loud is worth more than the trie itself.
Concurrency — the follow-up that decides the interview
"Now make it thread-safe" is asked at Amazon and Uber more often than not. The naive answer is one global lock. The graded answer names the trade-off:

rows: Default choice — matches the usual read-heavy mix
Deep trees with hot subtrees; hard to get right
Snapshot reads, backups, low write rate

blocks.title: `ConcurrentHashMap` alone is not enough
blocks.text: `createPath` is a **check-then-act** across two nodes: it reads the parent, then writes the child. Two threads creating `/a/b` and `/a/c` are fine; two threads both creating `/a/b` can both see it absent. Use `children.putIfAbsent(...)` and let the loser return `false` — that single call is what makes the operation atomic.
Scaling it up — where LLD meets HLD
If the interviewer pushes past the in-memory version, they are asking you to name the pieces a real filesystem adds. You are not implementing these; you are showing you know they exist.

blocks.title: From an in-memory trie to a real filesystem
blocks.caption: The trie survives as the *directory tree*. Everything else is added around it.
blocks.code:
flowchart LR subgraph M["In-memory (this problem)"] T["Segment trie
name → node"] end subgraph R["Real filesystem"] D["Directory entries
name → inode number"] I["Inode table
metadata, block pointers"] BA["Block allocator
free-space bitmap"] J["Journal / WAL
crash consistency"] C["Page cache
hot blocks"] end T -.->|"becomes"| D D --> I --> BA I --> J BA --> C

items: **Inodes** — split *name → id* from *id → metadata*. That indirection is what makes hard links possible: two names, one inode.
**Journaling / write-ahead log** — a `createPath` that dies halfway must not leave a directory entry pointing at nothing. Write intent, then apply.
**Block allocation** — files hold bytes, not one `int`. Extents or a free bitmap, plus indirect blocks for large files.
**Caching** — an LRU over hot path lookups turns repeated `get` on the same directory into a single map hit. This is where *Design LRU Cache* shows up inside this question.
**Sharding by path prefix** — distributed filesystems (HDFS, GFS) keep the namespace on a metadata server and shard the *data*, precisely because the tree is small and the bytes are not.

blocks.text: Follow-ups you should have an answer ready for

items.title: Implement `ls(path)` returning sorted children
items.text: Free in the trie: read `node.children.keySet()` and sort — O(c log c). Say the flat map needs a full scan. Then note that if `ls` is hot, a `TreeMap` per node keeps children sorted at insert time and makes `ls` O(c).

items.title: Delete a whole subtree
items.text: Unlink the child pointer from the parent — O(depth). The descendants become unreachable and are collected. In C++ you would need refcounting or an explicit post-order free.

items.title: Support `..`, `.` and a trailing `/`
items.text: Normalise into a segment stack before touching the trie: push a segment, pop on `..`, ignore `.` and empty segments. Keep it in one function so the core stays clean.

items.title: Return the longest existing prefix of a missing path
items.text: Walk until a child is missing and return how far you got — O(k), and impossible on the flat map without probing every prefix.

items.title: Autocomplete / prefix search on names
items.text: This is where a *character* trie inside each directory node earns its place — a second trie, nested, only if the interviewer asks.

items.title: Watch a directory for changes (inotify)
items.text: Observer pattern: a `List<Watcher>` on the node, notified on child insert or remove. Cheap to add because the structure already localises changes to one node.

items.title: Enforce a per-directory quota
items.text: Keep a subtree size on each node and update it along the insertion path — O(depth) per write, O(1) per read. Impossible to maintain cheaply on the flat map.

blocks.text: Edge cases to state before you are asked

items: `createPath("/", 1)` → `false`. The root is not a createable path.
`createPath("/a/b", 1)` when `/a` does not exist → `false`. No implicit `mkdir -p`.
`createPath("/a", 1)` twice → the second returns `false`; the stored value stays `1`.
`get("/a")` where `/a` exists only as the parent of `/a/b` → `-1`. This is the `hasValue` case.
`get` on a never-seen path → `-1`, not an exception.
Empty string, `//a`, and a trailing `/a/` → `false` from validation, not a crash.
Negative values are legal payloads — never overload `-1` as "absent".

blocks.text: Test cases
What you are graded on

rows: Asks whether `ls` is coming, then picks the structure
Names the exact operations that make it better, and the cost it adds
One `segments()` boundary, rest of the code trusts it
Shows `ls`/`delete`/quota falling out of the same structure

blocks.title: The 45-minute plan
blocks.text: **0–5 min** clarify and state the contract. **5–10 min** flat map, out loud, as the baseline. **10–15 min** name the operations that break it and pivot to the segment trie. **15–30 min** code `createPath`, `get`, `walk`, `segments`. **30–38 min** `ls`, `delete`, edge cases, tests. **38–45 min** concurrency and one scaling remark. Do not skip the baseline — pivoting *from* a working answer is the signal.
